text: x In living organisms, diffusion plays an important role in gaseous exchange between the cells as well as the cell and its external environment. x Exchange of O2 & CO2 in alveoli (millions of tiny, balloon-shaped air sacs in lungs) is an example of diffusion. x In a person suffering from pneumonia, the air sacs may fill with fluid or pus. This prevents diffusion of O2 & CO2 in alveoli (breathing issues in Coronavirus patients). PMF IAS – Learn Smart 46 Osmosis x Water obeys the law of diffusion. x Osmosis is the passage of water (diffusion of molecules of a solvent) from a region of low solute con- centration (hypotonic) through a semi-permeable membrane to a region of high solute concentration (hypertonic). x Semi permeable means that the membrane will allow small molecules and ions to pass through it but acts as a barrier to larger molecules or dissolved substances. x Thus, osmosis is a special case of diffusion through a selectively permeable membrane. x Unicellular freshwater organisms and most plant cells tend to gain water through osmosis. x Absorption of water by plant roots is also an example of osmosis. Reverse Osmosis (RO) x Reverse osmosis (RO) is a water purification technology that uses a semipermeable membrane to remove larger particles from drinking water. x In reverse osmosis, an applied pressure is used to overcome osmotic pressure so that pure water flows from a region of high solute concentration (hypertonic) through a semi-permeable membrane to a region of low solute concentration (hypotonic). PMF IAS – Learn Smart 47 Note: In NCERT Biology Compilation, I have given a wrong explanation for both Osmosis and Reverse Osmosis. What I have given here is the correct explanation. Application of Reverse Osmosis (RO) x RO was originally a technology devised in the late 1950s to desalinate sea water. x At present, it is possible to deploy a wide array of membranes and multiple stages of filters to filter a wide variety of solutes — arsenic, fluoride, hexavalent chromium, nitrates, bacteria. x This has led to an industry of home-RO systems for drinking water. x To create external pressure, RO relies on a pump and electric motors. x It uses “activated carbon” components, such as charcoal and carbon black that can filter out contami- nants as well as organic substances such as bacteria (UV light is also used to kill bacteria). x It all depends on the filtering material and the number of filters that incoming tap water must pass through. Problem with RO water purifiers PMF IAS – Learn Smart 48 x In making tap water pass through multiple stages of cleaning, RO systems end up wasting a lot of water. x Anywhere between three-five times more water is wasted by them (high carbon footprint). x RO system filters out essential micronutrients such as calcium, zinc, magnesium. Drinking such water over time could be harmful. x However, many manufacturers claim to overcome this challenge by “post-treatment” (added minerals). x RO system only reduces Total Dissolved Solids, ensure water is odourless and has a pH from 6.5-8.5. x The National Institute of Virology (NIV) claimed that most RO methods did not eliminate Hepatitis E virus. x However, a combination of filtration systems can eliminate most contaminants (more power consumption). x RO systems reduce the incentive for public-funded water distribution systems and vast majority of the coun- try can ill-afford such systems. x In case of sea water desalinization, deposition of brine (highly concentrated salt water) along the shores affects plankton, which is the main food for small fish species. How is the quality of piped water in the country? x Under the Jal Jeevan Mission, GOI has committed to provide tap water to the entire country by 2024. x However, studies show that the existing quality of piped water is deficient in much of India. x In Delhi, all tap water samples drawn from various places did not comply with the BIS’s requirements. x The case is the same with a lot of other cities. What is the quality of water globally? x Countries with a high development index tend to have good quality tap water. x Finland, Denmark, Germany, UK have access to freshwater lakes or glacier melt (clean and mineral rich). x Singapore and Israel rely on extensive recycling and even making sewage water fit for drinking. x But for much of the world, access to clean piped water from the public supply remains a challenge. Superconductor x A superconductor is a material that can conduct electricity (transport electrons) with zero resistance. x This means no heat, sound or any other form of energy would be released from a superconductor. x Hence, superconductors will help build highly efficient devices leading to huge energy savings. x Critical temperature (Tc) is the temperature at which the material becomes superconductive. x Critical temperature (Tc) for the currently developed superconductive materials is much below 0 °C. x Currently, a lot of energy must be used in the cooling process making superconductors uneconomical. x Applications: Maglev trains (in use), lossless long distance electrical transmission (futuristic application). PMF IAS – Learn Smart 49 Maglev trains x Maglev (magnetic levitation) trains use superconducting magnets to achieve levitation. x Superconducting magnets are electromagnets that are cooled to extreme temperatures during use. x They dramatically increase the power of the magnetic field. x In maglev trains, superconducting magnets suspend a train car above a concrete guideway. x Like ordinary magnets, these magnets repel one another when matching poles face each other. x The magnets employed (superconducting) and they can generate magnetic fields up to 10 times stronger than ordinary electromagnets, enough to suspend (levitate) and propel a train.
